A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdaLFL research. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, including readable equations, tables, and figures. Retained plots and relocated sections can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, learning curves, an inner-gradient-step ablation, runtime measurements, and learned-loss visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification results and adds regression experiments, comparator evaluations, and controlled analyses in Appendix D.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain offline initialization followed by online unrolled differentiation. The proposed loss network still has two 40-unit hidden layers with smooth leaky ReLU activations. New comparator and ablation implementations do not revise the core AdaLFL procedure.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from four image-classification datasets to include regression on Communities and Crime, Diabetes, and California Housing. These introduce continuous-target prediction across additional domains, with results in Table 1 and regression loss visualizations in Appendix E.

E2.justification: v2 adds Meta-LR comparisons in Table 3, online Quadratic-TP and Cubic-TP loss representations in Table 4, and explicit comparisons against both ReLU/SoftPlus and smooth-leaky-ReLU versions of offline ML3 in Table 5. This substantially expands the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce controlled variation of the adaptation target, loss representation, activation architecture, and training-versus-validation samples for meta-gradients. Regression uses mean squared error and an SGD learning rate of 0.001. Existing classification splits and stated classification hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.1–D.4 tests whether gains exceed learning-rate adaptation, depend on neural versus polynomial loss representations, arise from activation choice versus online optimization, and reflect validation-based regularization. The original inner-step ablation and classification loss visualizations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten independent executions with different seeds, matched base-model initializations, and mean ± standard deviation. v2 applies the same reporting practice to additional experiments without introducing new statistical tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds regression results and extensive comparator and ablation outcomes. For example, Table 3 reports Meta-LR outperforming AdaLFL on CIFAR-10/AllCNN-C, 0.0656 versus 0.0835 error. Retained classification AdaLFL scores are unchanged, but Table 1 changes ML3 on CIFAR-10/VGG-16 from 0.1027 ± 0.0062 to 0.1024 ± 0.0055.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 adds the explicit condition γ > 0 to the previously unqualified statement that the smooth leaky ReLU output is unbounded. The bilevel formulation and appendix activation derivation are retained; the additional Equation 11 merely expands the existing meta-gradient update.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims about online loss adaptation and improved training and inference. The conclusion modestly extends the explicit empirical claim from outperforming cross-entropy and ML3 to also outperforming the standard mean squared error loss.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds interpretations concerning information beyond learning-rate scaling, representation expressiveness, the relative contributions of activation choice and online optimization, and validation-induced regularization. It also discusses Meta-LR wins and polynomial divergence. However, D.2 overlooks the SVHN result favoring Cubic-TP when describing exceptions to neural-representation superiority.

D1.justification: v2 supplies Meta-LR initialization and adaptation pseudocode, regression learning-rate settings, and regression runtime measurements. Existing AdaLFL implementation details and hardware disclosures remain largely unchanged, and both versions retain a redacted code-link placeholder.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning PINN loss learning, loss-induced regularization, and combined meta-learning approaches, including Psaros, Gonzalez and Miikkulainen, Park and Oliva, Flennerhag, and Baik. The central offline-versus-online positioning remains unchanged. Raymond 2022 becoming Raymond 2023 is a publication update to the same work.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained with localized editing and reorganization. Sections 3.1–3.2 move to Appendix A, runtime analysis moves to Appendix D.5, and learning-rate scheduling moves into Section 5.4. The principal narrative and contribution structure remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and appendix text layout, expands Figure 3 with regression panels, adds Tables 3–6 and Figures 7–10, and expands and relocates the runtime table. Earlier appendix loss plots are retained as Figures 11–17. The new Figure 7 has a legend inconsistent with its caption.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited ability to separate online adaptation from learning-rate and activation effects through the new controlled comparisons in Appendix D. Regression experiments also strengthen evidence for applicability beyond classification. These gains in empirical scrutiny outweigh localized reporting problems, including Figure 7's inconsistent legend and D.2's overlooked SVHN exception; they do not depend on improved retained classification scores.
